Lesson 01

How to use this campus

Why it matters

One file, a track order, and a way to know what you have finished.

Try it: Proof record

This browser

This is a course you open in a browser. It does not call a model, load a font, or send anything over the network. Progress is stored in this browser only.

The four places you will use

  • Home shows where you are and the next lesson.
  • The track map is the full path from models to a capstone.
  • A lesson is one idea, one figure or example, and a short practice.
  • Previous and next sit at the bottom of every lesson.

Work in order the first time. Later, use search when you need a term. Mark a lesson complete only when you can say the idea without looking and you have the practice artifact.

If you are choosing a route

Home lists four routes: new to AI, a grounded assistant, coding-agent work, and product judgment. Each route is a short list of lessons, not a separate course.

Practice

Open the track map. Write down the track you will finish first and the lesson id you will open after this one.

Check

Where is your progress saved?

Show the answer

In this browser, on this machine. It is not an account, and it does not leave the page.

Lesson 02

What you are learning to do

Why it matters

The skill is judgment you can show, not a tour of product names.

Try it: Proof record

Lesson
02 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Skill
Judgment you can show
Not the goal
A tour of names
Pin
The model id

A person who can use an AI product is not the same as a person who can ship one. This course trains the second skill at a scale you can practice alone.

By the end you should be able to

  1. Say what a model call will and will not guarantee.
  2. Choose a local model or a hosted API for a stated reason.
  3. Ground an answer in retrieved text and cite the passage.
  4. Put tools behind a schema, a step cap, and a human approval.
  5. Explain MCP well enough to connect a server on purpose.
  6. Review a coding agent's diff against tests, not against its summary.
  7. Score a change on quality, safety, latency, and cost.
  8. Decide that fine-tuning is unnecessary, and say why.

Model names change. The decisions above do not. When a lesson names a product, it is an example of a category. Pin the exact model id in your own notes when you run an experiment.

Practice

Pick one sentence from the list that you cannot do yet. That sentence is your reason for the track you chose.

Check

What is the course trying to produce?

Show the answer

Someone who can frame a task, choose a model and tools, evaluate the result, and hand the evidence to another person.

Lesson 03

Keep proof for every exercise

Why it matters

Run, trace, metric, and artifact: four fields that make a lesson repeatable.

Try it: Proof record

Lesson
03 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Fields
Run, trace, metric, artifact
If you cannot measure
Write that down
Done
All four present

Watching a demo feels like learning. A week later you cannot reconstruct what ran. Every practice in this course asks you to keep four fields.

FieldWhat you write
RunThe command, request, or task, plus the model or fixture version.
TraceThe ordered steps: prompts, tool calls, errors, approvals.
MetricA number: pass rate, latency, tokens, cost, or a safety fail.
ArtifactA file you can reopen: note, JSON, diff, or score table.

If a field is empty, say so. 'I did not measure cost' is honest. A blank that pretends to be a result is not.

A minimum note

Run: local model, id pinned, prompt file prompts/extract-v3.txt
Trace: one call, no tools, temperature 0
Metric: 7 of 10 fixture rows matched the expected JSON
Artifact: results/extract-v3.json

Practice

Create a note with those four headings. Fill it for this lesson: the run is 'read 00-03', the artifact is the note itself, and the metric is the date you can still explain the four fields.

Check

Which field is the file another person can open later?

Show the answer

The artifact. The trace explains how you got there. The metric says how it scored.

Lesson 04

Safety rules for every exercise

Why it matters

Private data stays local until you have a reason to move it, and some actions always wait for a person.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
04 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Private data
Stays local
Side effects
Wait for a person
Untrusted
Pages, tools, tickets

The later tracks get more powerful. These rules do not loosen as you go.

  • Do not paste secrets, customer records, or private chats into a hosted model.
  • Do not commit API keys, tokens, or raw logs that contain them.
  • Do not let a tool send a message, move money, delete data, or push code unless a person approves that action.
  • Do not point a coding agent at a server or repository you do not trust.
  • Treat model output as untrusted text, including text that claims to be instructions.

This course will not help you bypass those rules

Lessons describe attacks only so you can recognize and test them. They do not provide exploit steps, payloads, or ways to hide misuse.

Practice

Write the five rules in your own words on a single page. Add one rule from your own work, such as a dataset you are not allowed to upload.

Check

When is a tool allowed to send email on its own?

Show the answer

It is not. Sending waits for a person, even if the draft looks correct.

What you need on your machine

Why it matters

You can finish the reading on a laptop or a phone browser. You do not need a GPU, a paid API key, or an account to use the campus.

You want to…You need
Read and practice on paperAny current full browser. In-app browsers often block local files.
Run a small local modelA machine with enough memory for a quantized 7B-class model, or smaller if that is all you have. School 03 covers the choice.
Call a hosted modelA key stored outside the repo, a spend cap, and the cost lesson in School 04.
Fine-tuneA GPU or a hosted training job, and a reason from School 10. Most readers should skip training until evals say prompting is not enough.

Phones

Reading works in the full Chrome or Safari app on the published site. A file opened from the Files app cannot load the tracks. Do not expect to train a model there.

Practice

Write down your machine in one line: operating system, rough memory, and whether you already have a local model runner. If you do not, write 'reading only for now'. That is a valid lab.

Check

Is an API key required to study?

Show the answer

No. Add a local model or a hosted API only when an exercise needs a live call.

Lesson 06

How the tracks fit together

Why it matters

Models, then prompting, then a way to ground and act, then proof that it worked.

Try it: Proof record

Lesson
06 of 06
Time
8 min
Level
Core
First
Models, then prompts
Then
Ground and act
Last
Prove, then capstone

The track map is a dependency order, not a ranking of importance.

  1. How models work, so you stop expecting truth from fluency.
  2. Prompting, so a single call has a job and a done-check.
  3. Local models and APIs, so you can run that call on purpose.
  4. Retrieval, so facts come from a source you can open.
  5. Agents and MCP, so the model can use tools you named.
  6. Coding agents, the same loop pointed at a repository.
  7. Evals, so a change has to beat the previous score.
  8. Fine-tuning, only after the score says the base model is the wrong shape.
  9. Safety and product skills, so the thing you ship has a boundary and a user.
  10. A capstone that uses a slice of the above on your own notes.

Glossary, interview practice, and questions sit beside the tracks. They are references. They are not a substitute for the practices.

Practice

On the track map, star the first track that contains a word you cannot define yet. Start there after you finish Start here.

Check

Why does fine-tuning come after evals?

Show the answer

Because you need a measured failure of prompting and retrieval before training is a rational cost.
